clues.title: Plate: long white, one blue strip on left
text: Spain uses standard long, **white** European plates with a single **blue strip** on the left.
NOTE: Most Portuguese plates have a yellow strip on the right. Italian plates have two blue strips on either side of the plate.
clues.summary: Standard long white European plates with a single blue strip on the left. Portuguese plates mostly have a yellow strip on the right, and Italian plates have two blue strips, one on each side.

clues.title: Bollard: yellow-orange reflector
text: The standard Spanish bollards have a **yellow-orange** reflector on the front and two white dots on the back (though the back can also be blank). They are typically hollow.
NOTE: Very close to Andorra, you can find a [slightly different bollard](https://goo.gl/maps/7zfsuvqVcq5xhuTJ7), which is also used in Andorra itself.
clues.summary: The standard bollard has a yellow-orange reflector on the front and two white dots (or nothing) on the back. They are usually hollow. Very close to Andorra a slightly different bollard is used, and also in Andorra.

differs.how: Near the border a slightly different bollard is used

clues.title: Pole: concrete ladder or wooden in rural areas
text: In Spain, you can find a variety of electricity poles and pole tops. In small towns and sparsely populated rural areas **concrete ladder poles** and **wooden poles** are the most common.
“Ladder” poles have indents that resemble a ladder, hence the name.
clues.summary: Many pole types exist. In small towns and sparse rural areas, concrete ladder poles (with ladder-like indents) and wooden poles are the most common.

clues.title: Pole: upside-down triangle top, upturned bar
text: “**French style**” poletops are common in Spain. They are shaped like an upside down triangle, with a horizontal top bar that is curved slightly upwards. They are usually found on top of tall ladder poles or [medium sized steel poles](https://goo.gl/maps/yWPof9m7EEy7o5u97).
NOTE: As the name suggests, French poletops are also very common in France.
clues.summary: "French style" pole tops shaped like an upside-down triangle with a slightly upward-curved top bar, on tall ladder poles or mid-size steel poles. Also very common in France.

clues.title: Power: many big pylons with high-voltage lines
text: High voltage electricity lines supported by **pylons** are very common in Spain, especially compared to other Mediterranean countries.
clues.summary: High-voltage lines on pylons are very common, even compared with other Mediterranean countries.

clues.title: Sign: road marker with colourful border
text: Spain has distinct road markers with a variety of **colourful borders**. The code on top is the number of the road.

NOTE: Andorra has [similar markers](https://goo.gl/maps/FEWfZhUVrr8EUTv28) and the letter codes preceding the road number on these markers are often an important region-specific clue. You can learn more about these codes in the region guessing section.
clues.summary: Distinct road markers with colourful borders, with the road number in the code on top. Andorra has similar markers, and the letters before the number are a key region clue.

clues.title: Sign: hunting signs
text: In rural areas you will often find hunting signs. There are two versions, both of which are unique to Spain. One is a simple white sign with a text starting with “coto” and ending in “caza”. The other one has a diagonally divided black and white background.

NOTE: These signs have an identifying [code](https://www.google.com/maps/@39.7437882,-5.9988875,3a,15y,62.89h,79.86t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1ssz27mavsgGpo566T_-XEmg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) that can sometimes be read. In this case “Ex” stands for Extremadura.
clues.summary: Rural hunting signs, unique here: a plain white one reading "coto ... caza", or one split diagonally black and white. A readable code on it can show the region ("Ex" is Extremadura).

clues.title: Guardrail: yellow reflectors on rounded A-type
text: Spain has **yellow reflectors** on rounded A-type guardrails.
NOTE: Belgium, Andorra, Gibraltar and most Latin American countries also have yellow reflectors. For a good overview of European guardrails, see [this infographic](/images/spain/europeguardrail.png).
clues.summary: Yellow reflectors on rounded A-type guardrails. Belgium, Andorra, Gibraltar and most Latin American countries have yellow reflectors too.

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian crossing with 8 stripes
text: Spanish pedestrian crossing signs have **8 stripes**. This is the highest number of stripes in Europe, and almost unique to Spain.
NOTE: The only other European country with 8 stripes is Andorra.
clues.summary: A crossing sign with 8 stripes, the most in Europe and almost unique to Spain. Andorra is the only other European country with 8.

clues.title: Sign: stop sign with small text
text: Spanish stop signs have a distinct **small** font.
NOTE: These are mostly useful to distinguish Portugal from Spain: Portuguese stop signs have a noticeably [larger](https://maps.app.goo.gl/fFE4hc7vSRj35Kc89) font.
clues.summary: Stop signs use a distinctly small font. This mostly separates it from Portugal, whose stop signs have a noticeably larger font.

differs.how: Portuguese stop sign font is noticeably larger

clues.title: Sign: red borders reach the edge of road signs
text: Red borders on road signs extend all the way to the edge of the sign. There is **no small white border** separating the red part from the edge.
NOTE: France, Italy and Portugal have a small [white](https://goo.gl/maps/qq8QB3ArzXtkz7sw5) border on the edge of such road signs.
clues.summary: The red border of road signs goes right to the sign's edge, with no thin white outer border. France, Italy and Portugal have a small white edge.

clues.title: Sign: flat signposts on most road signs
text: Almost all traffic signs, kilometre markers, chevrons and some direction signs in Spain have a **flat signpost**.
NOTE: Flat signposts in Europe are also present in Portugal, France and Andorra.
clues.summary: Almost all road signs, kilometre markers, chevrons and some direction signs sit on flat signposts. Portugal, France and Andorra have flat posts too.

clues.title: Chevron: black or blue with white arrows
text: Spain has two chevrons: **black with white** arrows, and **blue with white** arrows. Chevrons with a single arrow are rare.
NOTE:
- In Southern Europe, black with white chevrons can be found in Italy, Greece and Albania.
- France is the only other European country that has blue with white chevrons.
- Portugal has black with yellow chevrons.
clues.summary: Two chevrons: black with white arrows and blue with white arrows. Single-arrow chevrons are rare. Black-white ones also exist in Italy, Greece and Albania, blue-white only in France, and Portugal uses black with yellow.

differs.how: Portuguese chevrons are black with yellow arrows

clues.title: Sign: white direction signs with coloured road
text: Spanish direction signs have a white background. They often feature **colourful boxes** with road numbers, making them recognizable. These road number boxes can be many different colours.
Highway signs have a blue background.
clues.summary: White direction signs, often with colourful boxes showing road numbers in many colours. Highway signs are blue.

clues.title: Road lines: dashed outer lines on rural roads
text: Rural roads sometimes have **dashed outer lines**. This can help tell Spain apart from Portugal and Italy, where such road lines are (almost) non-existent.
Note that the reverse is not true: like Italy and Portugal, many Spanish roads do have solid outer lines.
clues.summary: Rural roads sometimes have dashed outer lines, which are almost nonexistent in Portugal and Italy. But many roads here have solid outer lines too, so only the dashed type is a clue.

differs.how: Dashed outer lines are almost nonexistent there
Dashed outer lines are almost nonexistent there

clues.title: Language: Spanish, ñ, de and del
text: **Spanish** is the main language in most of the country. It is a Romance language that is closely related to Portuguese.
Spanish and Portuguese can look very similar. Some key differences between the two:
- Ñ is unique to Spanish.
- Ç and lh are unique to Portuguese (Ç is also present in Catalan).
- Portuguese uses the -ao word ending, and -nh- instead of ñ.
- Spanish uses de and del, while these are often contracted to da, do, das and dos in Portuguese.
NOTE: Spain also has several regional languages, some of which are more common than Spanish in their respective regions. These languages are discussed in more detail in the region-guessing section.
clues.summary: Closely related to Portuguese. Ñ only exists in Spanish; Ç and lh are Portuguese (Ç is also Catalan). Portuguese uses -ao endings and -nh- instead of ñ, and contracts de to da, do, das, dos. Regional languages are covered separately.

differs.how: Portuguese has ç, lh, -ão, -nh- and da/do/dos

clues.title: Language: "calle" means street
text: The Spanish word for street is **calle**.
clues.summary: The Spanish word for street is calle.

clues.title: Sign: "Vado permanente" no-parking at garages
text: You will often find no parking signs in front of garage doors and gates. They will usually read “**Vado permanente**”.
These signs will very often have the name of the municipality after “Ayuntamiento de”.
NOTE: Italy uses signs that read “[Passo carrabile](https://maps.app.goo.gl/7zR6BMCLHRQb6cJQ7)”.
clues.summary: No-parking signs in front of garage doors and gates read "Vado permanente", often with the municipality after "Ayuntamiento de". Italy's say "Passo carrabile".

clues.title: Landscape: very diverse, forests to semi-desert
text: Spain has **highly diverse landscapes**, ranging from [lush Atlantic forests](https://goo.gl/maps/U8Vp3k1yGrLdVQANA) to [bone-dry semideserts](https://goo.gl/maps/PwTpyn5Lw6DMApWGA). Elevation is also varied: highland plateaus interspersed with [rolling hills](https://goo.gl/maps/hDzbVSrJbPSPQVnJ7) are common, but you might also encounter jagged mountain ranges and [very flat lowland](https://goo.gl/maps/kgiM3UXvKiQAcToWA) areas.
clues.summary: Highly varied: lush forests to bone-dry semi-desert, high plateaus with rolling hills, jagged mountains and very flat lowlands.

clues.title: Landscape: dry Mediterranean most places
text: While there is not one single definitive Spanish landscape, most of the country has a somewhat dry, **Mediterranean** climate, with matching vegetation and agriculture.
clues.summary: There is no single landscape, but most of the country has a fairly dry Mediterranean climate with matching plants and crops.

clues.title: Google car: Gen 3, antenna long, short or none
text: Generation 3 cars can have **long, short** or **no** antennas. The back of the car is usually not visible, but when it is, it can be either black or white.
NOTE: Coverage in Eastern Andalusia, Huesca, and Lleida sometimes has a long antenna with a [distinctive white top](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Hg7iR7rEuQNftXKe6).
clues.summary: Older Gen 3 cars (blurrier, softer colours) can have a long, short or no antenna. The back is usually hidden, but if visible it is black or white. East Andalusia, Huesca and Lleida sometimes have a long antenna with a white tip.

clues.title: Google car: blue or black Gen 4
text: Generation 4 cars are **blue** or less commonly **black**. The car can be completely hidden.
clues.summary: Newer Gen 4 cars are blue or, less often, black. The car can be completely hidden.

clues.title: Camera: low smallcam
text: Spain also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
clues.summary: Some Gen 4 smallcam coverage is mounted lower than usual, with a big round blur and a small front bump. The blur can be fully transparent and hard to spot.

clues.title: Camera: weird low-quality, wide round blur
text: Google used a weird, low-quality camera in Spain. This camera is known as the **official Ari** (or “Shitcam”). It has a wide circular car blur, and can be distinguished from Generation 2 by its lack of a sky halo and often somewhat brownish colours. A good map will not usually include this coverage, but it is good to be aware of its existence, in order to not be caught off-guard by it.
clues.summary: A strange low-quality camera (the Ari, or "shitcam") with a wide round car blur, no sky halo (which Gen 2 has) and often brownish colours. Good maps usually exclude it, but know it exists.

clues.title: Road numbers: letter codes show the region
text: Spanish regional road numbers feature **region-specific codes**. These are found on [road markers](https://goo.gl/maps/rhKLQGfHBrjwrCcVA), and sometimes on [direction signs](https://goo.gl/maps/3mEpJjQ2V7dRHXEb7).
For example, the [SG code on road markers](https://goo.gl/maps/1sgfM2413ykRU9P78) refers to a road in Segovia province.
The infographic shows almost all the regional codes, except for some very rare codes. Click on the image to enlarge it.
NOTE:
- National roads use the following codes: E, AP, A, R, N. These can be found anywhere in the country.
- Be careful: A is also used for community roads in Andalusia and Aragon.
- Some autonomous communities do not have community roads, only provincial roads. These have been indicated with grey on the map.
- Asturias uniquely has a large variety of local road codes.
- Ceuta only has N-roads. Melilla uses the code ML.
clues.summary: Regional road numbers carry region codes on markers and sometimes direction signs (for example SG is one province). National roads use E, AP, A, R, N anywhere. A is also used for regional roads in two regions. See the infographic for all codes.

clues.title: Phone numbers: landlines start 9 plus region
text: **Area codes** in Spain are very useful, as you only need two digits to get a very accurate guess. Every landline number starts with “9”, followed by the regional numbers.
Mobile numbers start with “6”, and are not relevant in region guessing.
clues.summary: Area codes are very useful: two digits give a very accurate guess. Landlines start with 9 followed by the regional digits. Mobiles start with 6 and don't help.

clues.title: Language: several regional languages
text: Spain has several regional languages. The ones that are most useful to GeoGuessr are **Catalan**, **Basque** and **Galician**.
Some other regions, such as Asturias, also have their own regional languages. But there, non-Spanish signage is much more rare.
clues.summary: The most useful for the game are Catalan, Basque and Galician. Other regions like Asturias have regional languages too, but non-Spanish signs are much rarer there.

clues.title: Language: Catalan, i for and, à è ò, ç
text: **Catalan** is a Romance language that is closely related to both Spanish and French.

It is spoken in Catalonia, the Valencian Community, and the Balearic Islands. In Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, it is (much) more common than Spanish on signage. The Valencian Community is more bilingual.
If you are unfamiliar with Romance languages, it can be hard to distinguish between Catalan and Spanish.
- The Catalan word for “and” is **i**, compared to Spanish y.
- The grave accent (**à, è, ò**), is exclusive to Catalan within Spain and very common to see in words, especially on à.
- The c with cedilla (**ç**) is also exclusive to Catalan within Spain.
clues.summary: A Romance language close to Spanish and French, much more common than Spanish on signs on the north-east coast and islands, more mixed in Valencia. Catalan uses i for "and" (Spanish y), grave accents à è ò, and ç, none of which Spanish uses.

clues.title: Language: "carrer" means street
text: The Catalan word for street is “**carrer**”.
clues.summary: The Catalan word for street is carrer. Seeing it instead of calle means a Catalan-speaking region (the north-east, Valencia or the Balearic Islands). Andorra uses Catalan too.

clues.title: Sign: "Gual permanent" no-parking
text: No parking signs in Catalan speaking areas will read “**Gual permanent**”. Most municipalities use “gual” in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands, while it’s more common to find a mix of Spanish and Catalan signs in Valencia.
clues.summary: In Catalan-speaking areas no-parking signs read "Gual permanent". Most municipalities in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands use "gual", while Valencia mixes Spanish and Catalan.

clues.title: Language: Basque, many Z and K
text: **Basque** is a language isolate that is spoken in the Basque Country and northern Navarre. In these regions, you will find a mix of Spanish and Basque signs (often bilingual).
Basque is not related to any other language, so it has a unique look. Z and K are common letters.
NOTE: Basque is also used in the border area of southwest France.
clues.summary: A language unrelated to any other, spoken in the Basque Country and northern Navarre, so signs are a mix of Spanish and Basque. Z and K are common letters. Also used across the border in southwest France.

clues.title: Language: "kalea" for street
text: Streets in Basque-speaking areas are sometimes called “**kalea**”. However, Spanish “calle” is also still common.
clues.summary: Streets in Basque-speaking areas are sometimes called "kalea", though "calle" is still common.

clues.title: Sign: bilingual sub-signs with thick black
text: Road signs in the Basque Country and Navarre often have these distinctive **bilingual sub-signs** with a **thick black border**.
Generally you will find Basque on top in the Basque Country, while it is more common to find Spanish on top in Navarre.
clues.summary: Road signs in the Basque Country and Navarre often have bilingual sub-signs with a thick black border. Basque is usually on top in the Basque Country, Spanish usually on top in Navarre.

clues.title: Language: Galician, ñ but no ç
text: **Galician** is a Romance language that is closely related to Portuguese. It is (unsurprisingly) spoken in Galicia. Compared to Catalan, it is less dominant, meaning you will still find a lot of Spanish-only signs in this region.
Galician can look very similar to Portuguese. Some ways to tell them apart is the use of **ñ** and the lack of **ç** in Galician.
clues.summary: A Romance language close to Portuguese, less dominant than Catalan, so many signs are Spanish only. Galician uses ñ and has no ç, which helps tell it from Portuguese.

differs.how: Portuguese has ç and no ñ

clues.title: Sign: "Rúa" with accent for street
text: Streets are commonly called **Rúa** in Galicia, whereas in Portugal they are called Rua (without an accent). However, you can sometimes find signs without the accent in Galicia.
clues.summary: Streets are commonly "Rúa" in this region, while Portugal writes "Rua" without an accent. Signs without the accent can still appear here.

differs.how: Portugal writes Rua without the accent

clues.title: Town names: begin with A, O, As or Os
text: Many **Galician town names** start with A, O, As or Os articles (examples: “A Pena”, “O Burgo”, “As Cruces”). This is both very common and unique to this region, and rarely over the border in western Asturias.
clues.summary: Many town names start with A, O, As or Os ("A Pena", "O Burgo", "As Cruces"). This is common and unique to the north-west, and rarely over the border in western Asturias.

clues.title: Flags: regional flags are common
text: The regional flags of the autonomous communities are reasonably common, so it is worth learning them.
NOTE: You can practise them with [this quiz](https://www.geoguessr.com/seterra/en/fl/2033).
clues.summary: Regional flags are fairly common, so they are worth learning.

clues.title: Flag: unofficial red-yellow striped
text: The Catalan Independence flag is not official, but is commonly found in Catalan-speaking areas. It uses the **red-and-yellow** striped [Senyera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senyera) pattern that is also used in four of the autonomous community flags.
clues.summary: The Catalan independence flag is unofficial but common in Catalan-speaking areas. It uses the red and yellow Senyera stripes that also appear in four regional flags.

clues.title: Landscape: very mountainous
text: Spain is a very **mountainous** country.
The highest mountain ranges are the Pyrenees in the northeast, and the Baetic System (which includes Sierra Nevada) in the southeast.

The Meseta Central is a high altitude, mostly flat area in the centre of the country. It is surrounded by several smaller mountain ranges: the Cantabrian Range in the north, the Iberian System in the east, and Sierra Morena in the south.
Within the Meseta Central there are two more mountain ranges: the Sistema Central (going from the Portuguese border to the northeast of Madrid) and Montes de Toledo.

There are four big river basins in Spain. The Tajo and Guadiana cross Extremadura and go into Portugal, the Guadalquivir covers most of the southwest of Andalusia and the Ebro river basin starts in Navarra and flows into the mediterranean in the south of Catalonia.
clues.summary: A very mountainous country. The highest ranges are in the northeast and southeast. A high, mostly flat plateau sits in the centre, ringed by smaller ranges, with two more ranges inside.

clues.title: Landscape: green lush hills, hedges and meadows
text: The landscape in the far north is much more **green and lush** than the rest of Spain. The landscape is generally quite hilly. Hedges and green meadows are common. In some places, this region’s landscape bears a vague resemblance to Ireland, France and the UK.
clues.summary: The far north is much greener and lusher than the rest, generally hilly, with hedges and green meadows. Some places look a bit like Ireland, France or the UK.

clues.title: Landscape: light grey rock, pines, rock walls
text: The **Pyrenees** is a large mountain range on the border between Spain and France. Its mountains are some of the highest in all of Spain. It can be recognized by its light grey rock and abundance of pine trees. Local architecture features many [rock walls](https://goo.gl/maps/F67y544xPUyR5ypo7).

NOTE: Andorra and the French part of the Pyrenees look very similar in terms of landscape and architecture. Also consider that the exclave of [Llívia](/images/spain/spain_pyreneesllivia.png) is part of Spain.
clues.summary: A big mountain range on the French border with some of the highest peaks, light grey rock, many pines and local buildings with rock walls. Andorra and the French side look very similar, and the exclave of Llívia is Spanish.

clues.title: Plants: thick forests of tall pines
text: Thick forests of **tall pines** can be found all throughout the Pyrenees. When encountered in smaller mountains in between grazing fields or agricultural land, it will most likely be in the Basque Country or Navarra.
clues.summary: Thick tall pine forests cover the mountains on the French border. In smaller mountains between grazing fields or farmland, you are most likely in the Basque Country or Navarra.

clues.title: Landscape: flat farmland, cereals, sunflowers
text: The centre of Castilla y León features a **mostly flat agricultural landscape**, with only slight changes in elevation. Most of the fields will have cereal crops like wheat and barley, and it is fairly common to find sunflower plantations.
clues.summary: The centre of Castilla y León is mostly flat farmland with slight height changes. Most fields grow wheat and barley, and sunflower fields are fairly common.

clues.title: Plants: vineyards between mountain ranges
text: Vineyards can be found in several places in Spain. However, if you see vineyards **in between mountain ranges** to the north and south, you are most likely in La Rioja.
clues.summary: Vineyards appear in several places, but vineyards between mountain ranges to the north and south mean La Rioja.

clues.title: Landscape: semi-desert strip, light sand
text: Starting in Navarra and cutting across the middle of Aragón, there is a strip of semi-desert landscape on both sides of the Ebro river basin. Light sandy soil and **small shrubs** growing on **small hills** are common in this area.
clues.summary: A strip of semi-desert on both sides of the Ebro basin, from Navarra across the middle of Aragón, with light sandy soil and small shrubs on small hills.

clues.title: Landscape: very arid, mostly flat
text: Very **arid** looking and mostly **flat** areas are common in central and south Aragón.
The soil is very white and rocky in the northern part. Red soil is more common in Teruel.
clues.summary: Very dry, mostly flat land in central and south Aragón. Soil is very white and rocky in the north and redder around Teruel.

clues.title: Landscape: totally flat land, vineyards, olives
text: Castilla la Mancha can have **completely flat landscapes**, which are not that common in Castilla y León. Half of Spain’s wine is produced in this region, so vineyards are fairly common.
In the western provinces of Ciudad Real and Toledo, it is very common to see olive tree plantations, generally in flatter ground than those found in Andalusia.
clues.summary: Castilla la Mancha can be completely flat, which is less common in Castilla y León. Half of the country's wine comes from here, so vineyards are common. In the western provinces of Ciudad Real and Toledo olive plantations are common, on flatter ground than in Andalusia.

clues.title: Plants: open fields with scattered holm and
text: Open fields sparsely populated with **holm oaks** ([Quercus ilex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercus_ilex)) and **cork oaks** ([Quercus suber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercus_suber)) are very common in Extremadura and neighbouring regions. These species of oaks tend to be on the smaller side, and have a Mediterranean look. Be careful not to confuse them with olive trees, as they can look superficially similar to the untrained eye.
North of Cáceres the vegetation is [more lush](https://goo.gl/maps/c2eY7SkHd8KcXn69A) and winter and spring coverage is more common.
clues.summary: Open fields sparsely dotted with small holm oaks and cork oaks, very common in Extremadura and nearby. They look Mediterranean and can resemble olive trees at first glance. North of Cáceres it is lusher and winter and spring coverage is more common.

clues.title: Landscape: arid, very sandy soil
text: In the southeast of Spain, especially in Murcia, you can find a rather **arid landscape**, with very sandy soil and **medium sized mountains** surrounding.
Small shrubs and small plantations of fruit trees and olive trees are a common sight around rural roads.
clues.summary: In the southeast, especially Murcia, a rather arid landscape with very sandy soil and medium-size mountains around. Small shrubs and small fruit or olive plantations are common by rural roads.

clues.title: Landscape: rugged bare mountains in haze
text: Mountains in this area, especially Murcia and the south of Alicante have a very distinct look.
They are quite **rugged**, usually lacking in vegetation. This region commonly features a **hazy** look, making mountains in the distance look like they are behind a sort of mist.
clues.summary: Mountains in Murcia and the south of Alicante look very distinct: rugged and mostly bare. The area is often hazy, so far mountains look like they are behind mist.

clues.title: Landscape: snowy peaks November to May
text: The mountain range of Sierra Nevada features **snowy peaks** through the months of November and May. Sierra Nevada is the only mountain range in south Spain with snow during most of the year.
clues.summary: The Sierra Nevada has snowy peaks from November through May, and is the only range in the south with snow most of the year.

clues.title: Towns: all-white houses on a mountainside
text: Towns built **on a mountain face**, consisting entirely of white houses, are very common on the south coast of Spain, around Málaga.
clues.summary: Towns of entirely white houses built on a mountain face are very common on the south coast around Málaga.

clues.title: Plants: olive trees across half the country
text: **Olive trees** are one of the main crops planted in Spain, they can be commonly seen in more than half of the country.
clues.summary: Olive trees are one of the main crops and can be seen in more than half of the country.

clues.title: Plants: endless olive groves on rolling hills
text: Around Córdoba and Jaén, you can find massive **olive tree plantations** growing over **rolling hills** and going as far as the eye can see.
The bigger and more remote plantations are usually only covered in [Generation 2](https://goo.gl/maps/kpRdHCFYG9cevzqG6).
clues.summary: Around Córdoba and Jaén, massive olive plantations spread over rolling hills as far as the eye can see. The bigger, more remote ones are usually only covered in Gen 2.

clues.title: Plants: olives in small or medium fields
text: South of Madrid, olive tree plantations are usually in small or medium sized fields, in mostly flat terrain and commonly accompanied by red soil.
clues.summary: South of Madrid, olive plantations are usually in small or medium fields on mostly flat ground, often with red soil.

clues.title: Plants: fenced olive groves or behind rock
text: Olive plantations on the east coast are commonly fenced or behind rock walls and you will almost always see mountains in some direction.
clues.summary: On the east coast, olive plantations are often fenced or behind rock walls, and you almost always see mountains in some direction.

clues.title: Plants: eucalyptus plantations
text: All throughout the north coast of Spain you will find **eucalyptus plantations** looking like this. Galicia has more plantations than the rest of the north combined.
NOTE: Eucalyptus plantations are also extremely common in Portugal.
clues.summary: Eucalyptus plantations are found all along the north coast, with more in Galicia than in the rest of the north combined. Also extremely common in Portugal.

clues.title: Plants: eucalyptus in dry land
text: When you encounter **eucalyptus trees in a dry environment**, you will most likely be in the province of Huelva. You can find them more rarely in Extremadura in the north and up until Córdoba in the east.
clues.summary: Eucalyptus trees in a dry setting most likely mean Huelva province. They are rarer in Extremadura to the north and as far east as Córdoba.

clues.title: Plants: orange groves in small valleys
text: On the east coast of Spain, you can find many **orange tree plantations**. They are usually in small valleys, and if they are in flat land you can usually see mountains to the west, north or south.
clues.summary: Many orange plantations on the east coast, usually in small valleys. On flat land you can usually see mountains to the west, north or south.

clues.title: Plants: orange groves on open flat land
text: In the Guadalquivir river basin you can also find many orange plantations, usually in much more open and flat terrain than those of the east coast.
There are some extensive [plantations](https://goo.gl/maps/6k7YejSEZE3tyhgu9) in the mountains, but coverage is sparse there.
clues.summary: In the Guadalquivir basin, many orange plantations on much more open and flat land than on the east coast. Some are in the mountains, but coverage is sparse there.

clues.title: Crops: corn in big river basins
text: **Corn** is most commonly grown in big river basins in Spain. It is also grown on the north coast, especially Galicia, and in an area in the north west of Castilla y León.
clues.summary: Corn is mostly grown in big river basins. It also grows on the north coast, especially Galicia, and in part of north-west Castilla y León.

clues.title: Plants: stone pine, fluffy, wide bulbous crown
text: **Stone pines** ([Pinus pinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_pine)) can be recognized by their fluffy leaves, and compact bulbous crown that is wider than it is tall.
Forests of exclusively stone pines in a flat area are very common around Valladolid and Huelva. It is common to see them in the mountains close to Barcelona in residential areas.
clues.summary: Stone pines have fluffy leaves and a compact bulb-shaped crown wider than tall. Pure stone pine forests on flat land are common around Valladolid and Huelva, and they appear in residential mountain areas near Barcelona.

clues.title: Plants: Aleppo pine, fluffy, messy crown
text: **Aleppo pines** ([Pinus halepensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_halepensis)) also have fluffy leaves, but their crown is less compact, more disorganised looking, and often taller, compared to stone pines.
This is the most common pine on the east coast of Spain and the Balearic Islands.
clues.summary: Aleppo pines are fluffy too, but their crown is looser, messier and often taller than a stone pine's. The most common pine on the east coast and Balearic Islands.

clues.title: Plants: tall thin pine, dark bark
text: **Baltic pines** ([Pinus sylvestris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_sylvestris)) are tall and thin, with a dark bark that sheds at the top, revealing the orange-red wood underneath. They usually do not have branches on the bottom half of the trunk, especially when fully grown.
Baltic pines can be found in mainly three mountain ranges: the Pyrinees, Sierra de Guadarrama and the Iberian System.
clues.summary: Scots pines are tall and thin, with dark bark that sheds near the top to show orange-red wood, and no branches on the lower half of the trunk when mature. Found mainly in the Pyrenees, the Sierra de Guadarrama and the Iberian System.

clues.title: Plants: maritime pine, grey-red bark
text: **Maritime pines** ([Pinus Pinaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_pinaster)) has two variants in Spain, near the Atlantic coast, it has grey bark with red undertones, and fluffy branches that point upwards. Older trees often don’t have any branches in the bottom half of the tree.
NOTE: Plantations of this pine are extremely common in north and central Portugal.
clues.summary: Near the Atlantic coast, maritime pines have grey bark with red undertones and fluffy upward-pointing branches, and older trees have no branches in the lower half. Plantations are extremely common in north and central Portugal.

clues.title: Plants: Mediterranean maritime pine
text: In the rest of Spain you can find the Mediterranean variant of the tree. It still has a grey bark with red tones, and it is usually very fissured.
You can find the tree in most of the mountain ranges in central and southern Spain. Extensive plantations in flat ground can be found North of [Segovia](https://goo.gl/maps/i6S6jEeFsbjheYQe6).
clues.summary: The Mediterranean variant has grey bark with red tones, usually deeply fissured. Found in most central and southern mountain ranges, with big plantations on flat ground north of Segovia.

clues.title: Road lines: outer line style
text: On small roads, particularly those without a middle line, roadlines can be a very good clue to determine where in the country a location can be.
- In places where straight outer lines are prevalent you will very rarely find dashed outer lines.
- In places where dashed outer lines are the main style, finding straight outer lines is rare, but less so than for the reverse.

Some provinces have their own style of roadline, such as [Araba](https://goo.gl/maps/Du77eErKjQhsXUfcA) where simple long dashed middle lines are the most common style, or [Gipuzkoa](https://goo.gl/maps/L9tZ6G8iXpTsExEx7), where you can see long outside dashes in roads with a middle line.
Catalonia also frequently features atypical roadlines but there is not one prevalent design.
clues.summary: On small roads without a centre line, edge-line style is a strong region clue. Where solid edges prevail, dashed ones are very rare. Where dashed prevail, solid ones are rare but less so.

clues.title: Road: rectangular or square km markers
text: Most kilometre markers in Spain are either rectangular or square in shape. This can be a good clue to exclude half the country if you can see one in the distance.
There are also some unique designs.
- [Andalusian](https://goo.gl/maps/QrMQ5BpvhHxxNRFw5) markers are especially tall, featuring an extra stripe with the name of the governing body responsible for the road.
- [Madrid](https://goo.gl/maps/do335gdysTZMqevC9) markers are square and feature the regional flag at the top.
- Markers in [Biscay](https://goo.gl/maps/DHoCAAiuBc1PfdtJ9) are bigger than usual and feature a semi-circle shape at the top.
NOTE: National roads will always have a [red rectangular marker](https://goo.gl/maps/UKUGZhzmPu8iTiFX7).
clues.summary: Most kilometre markers are rectangular or square, which can rule out half the country. Some unique designs: very tall ones with an extra stripe naming the road authority in Andalusia, square ones with the regional flag at the top in Madrid, and larger ones with a semicircle top in Biscay.

clues.title: Road: km marker with orange
text: Kilometre markers in Spain feature a coloured border. The standard colours, going from bigger to smaller roads, are **orange**, **green**, and **yellow**.
Some autonomous communities and provinces use different colours, or even unique designs altogether.
You can read more about the unique designs in this [document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Gm9yf5_530K5kGN00xe_GEW_43akMfKftBypJ8XXi2Y/edit#heading=h.c91f1i74w4l3).
clues.summary: Kilometre markers have a coloured border: standard colours are orange, green and yellow from bigger to smaller roads. Some regions and provinces use different colours or designs.

clues.title: Sign: green or blue top strip with municipality
text: Galician towns frequently use signs with a **green or blue strip** at the top featuring the name of the municipality.
NOTE: “Concello” is the Galician word for municipality, and exclusive to the region.
clues.summary: Towns often use signs with a green or blue strip at the top showing the municipality name. "Concello" is the word for municipality and is exclusive to the region.

clues.title: Bus stops: red post with CTA logo
text: Most bus stops in Asturias have a red post with the CTA logo at the top.
NOTE: These may be confused with [Madrid bus stops](https://maps.app.goo.gl/BUtYyixugRSHYbgR8), which can also have a red post. The company in charge of Madrid public transport goes by EMT.
clues.summary: Most bus stops in Asturias have a red post with the CTA logo on top. Madrid bus stops can be red too, but the operator there is EMT.

clues.title: Rubbish bins: COGERSA logo
text: Trash containers in Asturias frequently have the logo of COGERSA, the logo’s shape is distinct and can be recognized from afar.
NOTE: Recycling bins can also feature this logo.
clues.summary: Trash containers in Asturias often carry the COGERSA logo, a distinct shape visible from far away. Recycling bins can have it too.

clues.title: Pole: yellow snow poles with one or two
text: Yellow snow poles with one or two reflectors are unique to Asturias. They are usually found in the south of the region.
clues.summary: Yellow snow poles with one or two reflectors are unique to Asturias, usually in the south of the region.

clues.title: Bollard: short flat white stick
text: In Aragón, it is common to see this bollard design on regional roads.
It has a simple design, consisting of a short flat rectangular white stick with a grey reflector on both sides.
NOTE: There are [similar bollards](https://goo.gl/maps/S7WhiqK8rgF2caVt7) in other regions, but they appear much less frequently than in Aragón.
clues.summary: Common on regional roads in Aragón: a short, flat, rectangular white bollard with a grey reflector on both sides. Similar ones exist elsewhere but are far less frequent.

clues.title: Sign: round corrugated signposts
text: Many signs in Catalonia have **round, corrugated signposts**. This is especially common for direction signs. A similar design is also common in the [Basque Country](https://goo.gl/maps/7yJp32FEUtWj2mGp6) and the [Balearic Islands](https://goo.gl/maps/N8qyyoWVysXz7cKR6).
Note that municipalities may use signposts like this anywhere in the country, and that regular traffic signs retain the standard flat Spanish design.
NOTE: [French signs](https://goo.gl/maps/pQmg6fifZ3FEuJbi8) have a very similar design.
clues.summary: Many signs in Catalonia have round, corrugated signposts, especially direction signs. Also common in the Basque Country and Balearic Islands, and any municipality may use them. Regular traffic signs keep the flat Spanish design. French signs look very similar.

clues.title: Sign: hunting sign "Àrea privada de Caça"
text: In Catalonia and sometimes the Balearic Islands you will find huntings signs in Catalan, usually reading “**Àrea privada de Caça**”.
clues.summary: In Catalonia and sometimes the Balearic Islands, hunting signs in Catalan, usually "Àrea privada de Caça".

clues.title: Bollard: squarer orange reflector
text: Within mainland Spain, this bollard is almost exclusive to the provinces of Lleida and Tarragona in Catalonia.

It features a more **square and orange reflector** on the front, compared to the standard Spanish bollard design. There is a **white reflector** on the back, instead of the two dots of standard bollards.
Some toll highways like the [AP-6](https://goo.gl/maps/Ce7fFoD835ZTPKzf7) also use this design.
NOTE: This bollard can also be found on the [eastern half of the Canary Islands](https://goo.gl/maps/uSyWhSZcGbTVX4dU8).
clues.summary: On the mainland almost only in Lleida and Tarragona: a squarer orange reflector on the front and one white reflector on the back instead of two dots. Some toll highways such as the AP-6 use it too, and so does the eastern half of the Canary Islands.

clues.title: Chevron: big square, single arrow
text: Big square chevrons with a **single arrow** are commonly found in Catalonia.
clues.summary: Big square chevrons with a single arrow are common in Catalonia.

clues.title: Chevron: small square, red arrow on white
text: Small square chevrons with a **red arrow** on a white background are exclusive to Murcia.
clues.summary: Small square chevrons with a red arrow on white exist only in Murcia.

clues.title: Bus stops: round-topped red stops, green buses
text: The surrounding region of Madrid has round topped **red bus stops**, and **green buses**. Some bus stops are just a [red post](https://goo.gl/maps/gtNJEs9Bswb7QT9PA).
In the city centre, you can find urban blue buses.
clues.summary: Around the capital, bus stops have round red tops and buses are green. Some stops are just a red post. In the city centre buses are blue.

clues.title: Bollard: standard with green top
text: In the region of Extremadura, it is common to see the normal Spanish bollards with **green tops**. This bollard variant is exclusive to this region.
clues.summary: In Extremadura the normal Spanish bollards often have green tops, a variant unique to the region.

clues.title: Field markers: stone with blue left half
text: In Castilla la Mancha you can find stone markers with the region’s [coat of arms](https://brandemia.org/sites/default/files/inline/images/logo_castilla_antes.jpg) lining up fields. It can be recognized from afar by the blue coloured left side and the unpainted right side.
clues.summary: In Castilla la Mancha, stone markers with the regional coat of arms line fields. They are recognisable from afar by the blue left side and unpainted right side.

clues.title: Pole: steel mesh with rectangles, not triangles
text: Poles with a **steel mesh** structure making **rectangular shapes** instead of the typical triangles can be found in the southern half of Spain, and are particularly common in Murcia and southern Alicante.
clues.summary: Poles whose steel mesh forms rectangles instead of the usual triangles, in the southern half, especially Murcia and southern Alicante.

clues.title: Sign: government signs with green stripe on
text: Signs from the local government of Andalusia are very recognizable because of the **green stripe** on the left side.
It is also very common to see small versions of these signs around nature reserves with **green signposts**.
clues.summary: Signs from the Andalusian regional government have a green stripe on the left. Small versions on green signposts often mark nature reserves.

clues.title: Pole: blue and yellow snow poles
text: **Blue and yellow snow poles** are unique to Andalusia.
clues.summary: Blue and yellow snow poles are unique to Andalusia.

clues.title: Roofs: almost black slate roofs
text: There is a large part of north-west Spain where you will find almost exclusively **slate roofs** (recognisable by their almost black colour). This type of roofing can be seen sparingly all the way to the west coast of Galicia, but ends rather abruptly on the east.
Slate roofs can also be found in the [Pyrenees](https://goo.gl/maps/gEG616kL4GBMD2HV8) near Andorra, and in the [mountain ranges](https://goo.gl/maps/WF1eMyRmBBnrFF867) north east of Madrid.
clues.summary: A large part of the north-west has almost only slate roofs (nearly black). They reach the west coast of Galicia but stop abruptly in the east. Slate roofs also appear in the Pyrenees near Andorra and in the mountains northeast of Madrid.

differs.how: Slate roofs appear near Andorra in the Pyrenees too

clues.title: Houses: big concrete blocks
text: Many houses in Galicia are built with **big concrete blocks**, sometimes textured to resemble natural stone.
Plain concrete blocks are also an extremely common material for [walls](https://goo.gl/maps/rPpmQLWq37euCkuJ9) and miscellaneous buildings like [garages](https://maps.app.goo.gl/nwbdKGLUKSJGjp7FA).
clues.summary: Many houses in Galicia are built with big concrete blocks, sometimes textured like natural stone. Plain concrete blocks are also very common for walls and garages.

clues.title: Buildings: narrow raised granary (horreo)
text: In Galicia, these unique **granaries** called “horreos gallegos”, or “cabazos”, are very common. Note that they can be made from various materials, but the shape remains the same.
clues.summary: In Galicia, unique raised granaries called horreos gallegos or cabazos are very common. They can be of different materials but always have the same shape.

clues.title: Buildings: big square granary on four pillars
text: In Asturias, “hórreos” are bigger, generally with a square design, and are built above four pillars, with or without walls. You will sometimes find a **rectangular** variation, usually built on top of six or eight pillars called “[panera](https://goo.gl/maps/drVo2HBDcETz5TY68)”.
If you find an “horreo” with a slate roof, you will be in western Asturias.
clues.summary: In Asturias, hórreos are bigger, usually square and on four pillars, with or without walls. A rectangular version on six or eight pillars is called a panera. A slate roof means western Asturias.

clues.title: Houses: large white with wooden frames
text: **Large white houses** with wooden frames are common in the Basque Country, the Basque part of Navarra, and Cantabria.
clues.summary: Large white houses with wooden frames are common in the Basque Country, the Basque part of Navarra and Cantabria.

clues.title: Houses: isolated stone farmhouses (masías)
text: Traditional farm houses called “[masías](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masia)” are common in Catalonia, eastern Aragón and parts of the Valencian Community.
They are usually made of stone and stand isolated or as part of a small complex.
clues.summary: Traditional stone farmhouses called masías, standing alone or in a small group, are common in Catalonia, eastern Aragón and parts of Valencia.

clues.title: Towns: whole towns of white-painted houses
text: Within the centre and south of Spain, towns made **completely** out of **white painted houses** are very common in Andalucía and Extremadura.
You can still see a fair amount of white painted houses in Castilla la Mancha but streets where every house is white will not be common.
clues.summary: In the centre and south, towns made fully of white houses are very common in Andalucía and Extremadura. Castilla la Mancha has many white houses too, but streets where every house is white are uncommon.

clues.title: Google car: black, no antenna
text: In Asturias you can find a **black** car with **no antenna** and a visible brake light.
NOTE: This car can very rarely spill into neighbour regions like [Galicia](https://goo.gl/maps/NrhqCAJyCAzVSnb69).
clues.summary: In Asturias, a black car with no antenna and a visible brake light. It can very rarely spill into neighbouring regions like Galicia.

clues.title: Google car: Gen 3 antenna with white top
text: You can sometimes find a special Generation 3 antenna with a distinctive **white top**, similar to the one found in Gibraltar.
This antenna is found in the eastern half of Andalusia and in the provinces of Huesca and Lleida in the northeast of the country.
clues.summary: A special Gen 3 antenna with a white top, like Gibraltar's, in the eastern half of Andalusia and the provinces of Huesca and Lleida.

clues.title: Landscape: dry coastal pine hills
text: The **Balearic islands** have a recognizable, coastal Mediterranean look. Somewhat dry looking forests of Aleppo pines cover most of the hills, and small patches of agricultural land, mainly with fruit trees and olive trees, cover the flatter areas between towns.
clues.summary: A coastal Mediterranean look: somewhat dry Aleppo pine forests on most hills, with small patches of farmland (mainly fruit and olive trees) on flatter ground between towns.

clues.title: Walls: low rock walls everywhere
text: Low **rock walls** are extremely common on the Balearic Islands.

NOTE: Another Mediterranean region with a similar amount of rock walls is the area around Bari in Italy. This region can sometimes [look similar](https://goo.gl/maps/f2TAiSPiTVn5uNco6) to the Balearic Islands.
clues.summary: Low rock walls are extremely common on the Balearic Islands. The area around Bari in Italy has a similar amount and can look alike.

differs.how: Bari area has similar walls and can look alike

clues.title: Houses: fully white
text: The stereotypical Balearic house is painted completely **white**. You can find flat roofs, but tiled roofs with a small incline are the most common.
clues.summary: The typical Balearic house is painted completely white. Flat roofs exist, but low-pitched tiled roofs are the most common.

clues.title: Landscape: grazing fields on one island
text: Within the Balearic Islands, **grazing fields** are almost exclusive to the island of Menorca.
clues.summary: Within the Balearic Islands, grazing fields are almost exclusive to Menorca.

clues.title: Landscape: low coastal shrubs
text: The small island of Formentera frequently features low **coastal shrubs**. It is common to be able to see the mountains of Ibiza from Formentera’s north coast.
clues.summary: Formentera often shows low coastal shrubs, and the mountains of Ibiza can often be seen from its north coast.

clues.title: Landscape: tall mountain range to the northwest
text: The north-west of Mallorca has a **tall mountain range** that can be seen from many places on the island. It is the only island in the Balearics with mountains this big.
clues.summary: The north-west of Mallorca has a tall mountain range seen from many places on the island, the only Balearic island with mountains this big.

clues.title: Islands: archipelago off west Africa
text: The **Canary Islands** (or Canaries for short) are a Spanish archipelago off the west coast of Africa. Because they are so far away from mainland Spain, being able to consistently recognize them is important for your scores.
NOTE: Do not confuse their location with the nearby Portuguese island groups of the Azores and Madeira.
clues.summary: The Canary Islands are a Spanish archipelago off the west coast of Africa, far from the mainland, so recognising them matters for your score. Don't confuse them with the Portuguese Azores and Madeira.

differs.how: Azores and Madeira are Portuguese island groups nearby

clues.title: Landscape: very diverse, volcanic, pines, arid
text: The Canaries have **extremely diverse landscapes**, including [steep mountains](https://goo.gl/maps/rfH1kBDye8h9rWaS6), [pine forests](https://goo.gl/maps/Bn6ErCKJ3sfiUaUa8), [volcanic soil](https://goo.gl/maps/6JqQk3AxRiRF3WoDA), and [extreme aridity](https://goo.gl/maps/4fdpWvUUTJYxJMEd7). You can also encounter [more normal landscapes](https://goo.gl/maps/zVYFchUyxrDQ7uyx5) that can look more like mainland Spain.

NOTE: Because of its diversity, it is hard to pin down the average landscape in the Canaries. A more useful strategy is to focus on whether it looks unique and unlike anything that you would find in mainland Europe: if meta matches with Spain, but something is “off” in terms of vibe, consider the Canaries.
clues.summary: Extremely varied: steep mountains, pine forests, volcanic soil and extreme dryness, though some places look like mainland Spain. Look for something that feels off compared with mainland Europe even when the other clues say Spain.

clues.title: Landscape: dark exposed volcanic soil
text: In some parts of the island of **Lanzarote** on the Canary Islands, a very dark, exposed volcanic soil can be seen. In places, this landscape superficially resembles the surface of the moon.
NOTE: The other Canary Islands can sometimes have similar landscapes as well, but it is by far the most common on Lanzarote.
clues.summary: On Lanzarote, very dark, bare volcanic soil that can look like the moon. Other Canary islands can look similar, but it is by far the most common here.

clues.title: Landscape: very arid, little plants
text: The island of **Fuerteventura** in the Canary Islands is characterised by a very arid landscape with little to no vegetation. Orange soil is very common, and within the Canary Islands archipelago essentially unique to this island.
clues.summary: Fuerteventura is very arid with almost no vegetation. Orange soil is common and essentially unique to this island among the Canaries.

clues.title: Bollard: squarer orange reflector
text: This **unique bollard design** is extremely common in the province of Las Palmas (which includes the islands of Gran Canaria, Fuerteventura and Lanzarote).
It features a more square and orange reflector on the front, compared to the standard Spanish bollard design. There is a white reflector on the back, instead of the two dots of standard bollards.
This bollard can also be found on mainland Spain, in the provinces of Lleida and Tarragona.

NOTE: The province of Santa Cruz de Tenerife (which includes the islands of Tenerife, La Gomera, El Hierro and La Palma) only uses bollards on highways, with the [standard Spanish design](https://goo.gl/maps/KXVo954u8dnxg5dy5).
clues.summary: Extremely common in Las Palmas province (Gran Canaria, Fuerteventura, Lanzarote): a squarer orange reflector on the front and a white reflector at the back instead of two dots. Also in Lleida and Tarragona on the mainland. Tenerife province only has standard bollards, on highways.

clues.title: Plants: vines in volcanic soil behind
text: You can find these **unique wine plantations** with volcanic soil and rocks in the shape of a semicircle on the island of Lanzarote.
clues.summary: Unique vineyards in volcanic soil with semicircular rock walls, on Lanzarote.

clues.title: Landscape: barren island, always overcast
text: Off the north coast of Lanzarote, you will find the small island of **La Graciosa**. The island’s landscape is completely barren, and the entire coverage features **overcast weather**. There are two towns on the south coast of the island, with white flat-roofed houses like the east Canaries.
clues.summary: The small island of La Graciosa, off Lanzarote's north coast, is completely barren and all coverage is overcast. Two towns on the south coast have white flat-roofed houses like the eastern Canaries.

clues.title: Coverage: two exclaves in North Africa
text: The two Spanish enclaves of **Ceuta **and** Melilla** in North Africa, which are partially surrounded by Morocco, both have coverage. They often catch beginning players off-guard, so it is good to be aware of them and their location.
clues.summary: Two Spanish enclaves in North Africa, partly surrounded by Morocco, have coverage. They often surprise new players, so know they exist.

clues.title: Houses: flat roofs in warm pale yellow to red
text: Ceuta features north African architecture, consisting of mainly flat roofed houses in warm colours, ranging from pale yellow to red.
Almost all of the Generation 4 coverage in Ceuta features a **bright blue sky** in sunny weather with occasional clouds.
clues.summary: Ceuta has north African architecture: mostly flat-roofed houses in warm colours from pale yellow to red. Almost all Gen 4 coverage has a bright blue sky in sunny weather with occasional clouds.

clues.title: Landscape: mountainous Mediterranean
text: You will find a **mountainous, mediterranean** landscape in Ceuta, featuring a mix of eucalyptus trees and pines.
clues.summary: A mountainous Mediterranean landscape with a mix of eucalyptus and pines in Ceuta.

clues.title: Guardrail: black and white
text: Within Spain, **black and white guardrails** are unique to Ceuta.
clues.summary: Within Spain, black and white guardrails are found only in Ceuta.

clues.title: Houses: north African style, hazy and overcast
text: Melilla also features similar North African architecture. The coverage in Melilla has a **hazy** look, with a significantly less saturated sky than Ceuta. Most of the coverage is cloudy or overcast.
Melilla has little rural coverage, mainly by the [Morocco-Spain border](https://goo.gl/maps/MEvyBFFYmeHYiDhw6).
clues.summary: Melilla has similar north African architecture. Its coverage looks hazy with a much less saturated sky than Ceuta and is mostly cloudy or overcast. There is little rural coverage, mainly by the Morocco border.

clues.title: Sign: yellow scallop shell on blue
text: The [**Camino de Santiago**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camino_de_Santiago) (the **Way of St. James** in English), is a network of pilgrim's ways across Europe leading to the shrine of apostle James (Santiago in Spanish) in Santiago de Compostela.

These paths are frequently marked with a yellow [scallop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scallop#Shell_of_Saint_James) on a blue background. Markers can be found both in traffic signs and in waystones.
It is common to see [pilgrims](https://goo.gl/maps/q2VozCDJbQbpZVVdA) hiking or biking along these routes, particularly during the summer.
NOTE: Markers for it can be found all over Europe, going as far as [Lithuania](https://maps.app.goo.gl/iEqTRA9J3qYRgtGV6), but are much more common the closer you are to Santiago.
clues.summary: The Camino de Santiago pilgrim routes are marked with a yellow scallop on blue, on traffic signs and waystones. Pilgrims often hike or bike here, especially in summer. Markers exist across Europe, even Lithuania, but are far more common near Santiago de Compostela.

differs.how: Markers appear there but are much rarer

clues.title: Coverage: early-spring dirt roads, green grass
text: Coverage during early spring on dirt roads between green grassy fields, and leafless vineyards with red soil, is very common in the central-north part of Castilla la Mancha.
This type of coverage is particularly extensive in the northern part and exclusively in generation 3. Towards the south you will also find very similar looking coverage in generation 4.
clues.summary: In north-central Castilla la Mancha, early spring coverage on dirt roads between green grassy fields and leafless vineyards on red soil is very common, especially in the north and only Gen 3. Further south similar Gen 4 coverage exists.

clues.title: Bollard: flat with square red reflector
text: The AP-15 in Navarra features unique bollards with a simple flat design and a square red reflector. Guardrails also have [red reflectors](https://maps.app.goo.gl/c9X1ak7KB5EhdDqRA) unlike the rest of Spain.
clues.summary: The AP-15 in Navarra has unique simple flat bollards with a square red reflector, and guardrails there have red reflectors unlike the rest of the country.

clues.title: Taxi: black with yellow doors
text: Taxis in Barcelona are black with yellow doors, including the trunk door.
clues.summary: Taxis in Barcelona are black with yellow doors, including the trunk door.

clues.title: Landscape: extremely flat delta
text: The Ebro delta (Deltebre in catalan) features an extremely **flat **landscape, where **rice fields** and **water canals** are very common.
There are significant mountains to the South, West, and North, and some of them can be seen from almost every location in the delta.

clues.title: Language: Aranese, carrèr, avenguda, passeg
text: Aranese is a language spoken only by about 2,800 people in Val d'Aran (Catalonia region of Spain west of Andorra on French border), most notably the town of Vielha. It looks very similar to Catalan and the street names are the easiest way of identifying it. Although uncommon recognizing it could give you an easy high scoring guess.
**carrèr** - (carrer in Catalan, look for the accent on the "e")
**avenguda** - (avinguda in Catalan)
**passeg** - (passeig in Catalan)
Other clues that may help you guess Val d'Aran is that it is a mountainous region with many rock buildings similar to Andorra.

clues.title: Language: ñ, ¿ ¡, y, -ción, -miento, ll
text: Here are some general tips to recognize Spanish:
Ñ is ALMOST unique to Spnaish (exception = Galician)
¿ ¡ inverted question and exclamation marks are common
and = "y"
Some words frequently used: de, el, del, los, la(s), uno(s), una(s)
Word endings: -o, -a, -ción, -miento, -dad
double l "ll" more common than other romance languages (Catalan exception)
